{"id": "2:22/q56", "question": "How is rational argument for faith defended?", "turns_on": "The notes give different senses, parses, reports, or grounds for this point.", "positions": [{"id": "2:22/q56/p1", "position": "Prophets and scripture use reasoned proofs for oneness, prophethood, and resurrection.", "reasons": "RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p74#2/r3]: Al-Rāzī introduces the following verses as an argument establishing divine unity, prophethood, and resurrection. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p75/r1]: After describing believers, unbelievers, and hypocrites, God shifts from speaking about them to addressing them directly, an iltifāt also seen in 1:5. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p75/r2]: Direct address stirs and moves the hearer more than continuing to speak about that person in the third person. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p75/r3]: The shift honors and draws the addressee near: after initially making the Messenger an intermediary, God now addresses the person without an intermediary. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p75/r4]: The move from third to direct address suggests that a servant engaged in worship is continually ascending. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p75/r5]: Because the earlier verses narrated their condition and these verses impose difficult commands, God’s direct personal address gives relief and makes the burden pleasant. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p75/r6]: ʿAlqama and al-Ḥasan say that Qur’anic addresses “O people” are Meccan, while “O you who believe” is Medinan. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p75/r7]: Al-Qāḍī accepts that distinction if it rests on transmitted reports, but rejects deriving it merely from the larger number of believers in Medina: believers may be addressed as people, and unbelievers may be commanded to worship just as believers are told to persist and increase in worship. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p76#2/r1]: Ay connects the vocative to a noun bearing the definite article, just as dhū and alladhī connect generic nouns to descriptions and definite nouns to clauses; ay is ambiguous and needs a noun or equivalent adjective to specify it. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p76#2/r2]: The vocative particle governs ay, while the following noun is its adjective, as in “O Zayd, the courteous”; unlike Zayd, ay cannot stand independently and therefore remains joined to its adjective and described noun. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p76#2/r3]: The inserted attention particle reinforces the call and compensates for the genitive construction expected with ay. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p76#2/r4]: The emphatic formula is frequent in the Qur’an because its commands, prohibitions, promises, threats, and momentous histories must awaken listeners who are heedless. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p76/r1]: Words normally denote linguistic or nonlinguistic things; the vocative particle is different, functioning as an act that draws attention rather than denoting another thing. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p76/r2]: “O Zayd” cannot mean “I call Zayd”: the latter is a truth-apt report, does not itself make Zayd the addressee, may be spoken to a third party, and reports rather than performs the call. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p76/r3]: Though names are strongest and particles weakest, a name can join a particle in calling; by analogy, a human can serve the transcendent Lord through invocation and humble supplication. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p76/r4]: Yā originally calls someone distant; hamza (a-) calls someone near. Using yā for someone nearby treats an inattentive or heedless person as distant. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p76/r5]: Although God is nearer than the jugular vein, a supplicant says “O Lord” either from humility and self-reproach, distancing himself from the stations of intimacy, or because answering prayer is supremely important. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p80/r10]: Rāzī turns to Qur’anic proofs of divine transcendence, maintaining that God is neither a body nor located in space. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p80/r4]: Rāzī identifies five proofs of the Creator in these verses: creating accountable people, their predecessors, heaven, earth, and fruits from rain sent down from heaven. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p80/r5]: The Qur’an’s other signs in the heavens and earth likewise aim to establish the Creator’s existence. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p80/r9]: Different fruits and animals arising despite shared four-element natures show that God is powerful and freely choosing, not acting by intrinsic necessity. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r1]: As evidence for transcendence, Rāzī cites God’s proof given to Abraham against his people. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r10]: When Pharaoh demanded another proof, Moses named the Lord of the East and West. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r11]: These proofs belong to the prophets’ practice: they reasoned them out and inherited them from their purified predecessors. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r12]: Moses also argued for his prophethood by offering a clear miracle as evidence of his truthfulness. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r13]: Muhammad’s argument for monotheism, prophethood, and resurrection is unmistakable because the Qur’an is full of such proofs. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r14]: The Qur’an refutes materialists who say only time destroys by presenting various proofs. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r15]: Varied plants and animals arising despite shared natural temperaments and celestial influences refute those who deny a freely choosing Creator. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r16]: Abraham’s argument when night covered him refutes those who make celestial bodies partners by claiming they influence the world. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r17]: The Qur’an also refutes lower partners: Christians claim divinity for Christ and idolaters for their idols. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r18]: One group denied prophethood altogether, asking whether God would send a human messenger. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r19]: Another group, including Jews and Christians, accepted prophethood in general but challenged Muhammad’s prophethood; the Qur’an answers their objections. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r2]: Abraham challenged his father’s worship of an idol that could neither hear, see, nor help him. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r20]: When critics objected to Qur’anic parables, God replied that He is not ashamed to give even a mosquito as an example. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r21]: When critics demanded further miracles, including a spring from the earth, the Qur’an answered their challenge. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r22]: When critics objected to gradual revelation as grounds for suspicion, God explained that it strengthened the Prophet’s heart. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r3]: Abraham verbally challenged his people about the statues to which they were devoted. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r4]: Abraham demonstrated the idols’ impotence by smashing them all except the largest, so that the people might turn to it. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r5]: Before the ruler, Abraham argued that his Lord gives life and death, exposing the ruler’s claim to do the same. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r6]: Rāzī says sound minds recognize that kalām merely presents these prophetic proofs and answers objections to them. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r7]: Abraham also asked God to show him how He revives the dead, addressing the afterlife. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r8]: Moses answered Pharaoh with the Lord who gave each thing its form and guidance, the same creation-and-guidance proof Abraham used of God creating and guiding him. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r9]: Moses’ appeal to the Lord of Pharaoh’s forefathers echoes Abraham’s argument that his Lord gives life and death. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p83/r1]: The Qur’an answers those who dispute resurrection with many proofs for the resurrection and against its deniers. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p83/r10]: The Qur’an condemns arguing about God without knowledge, which implies that argument grounded in knowledge is not blameworthy and is praiseworthy. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p83/r2]: To those who say obligations bring no benefit, God replies that good or evil deeds return to the doer. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p83/r3]: To the claim that determinism invalidates obligation, God replies that He is not questioned about what He does, while people are questioned. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p83/r4]: Rāzī abbreviates these examples because their full treatment appears elsewhere in the book. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p83/r5]: Since every prophet practiced this discipline, Rāzī concludes that its critic is either an unbeliever or ignorant. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p83/r6]: Rationally, taqlīd cannot justify choosing one authority: following everyone entails following unbelievers, choosing only some has no basis, and rejecting all imitation leaves rational inquiry. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p83/r7]: Scripture commands calling to God with wisdom and good admonition and debating in the best manner; Rāzī interprets wisdom as proof and demonstration. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p83/r8]: The commanded debate concerns monotheism and prophethood, not legal branches: such branches are pointless to those rejecting prophecy, while those accepting it would not dispute the Prophet. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p83/r9]: Because Muslims are commanded to follow Muhammad and take him as their example, they too must engage in the debate he was commanded to conduct. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p89#2/r10]: Celestial and elemental bodies share corporeality, so their differing quantities, shapes, and locations cannot be explained by corporeality or any property necessarily belonging to it. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p89#2/r4]: The possibility of attributes is inferred from the heavens and earth’s created arrangement; Rāzī specifically points to the earth as a resting-place and sky as a structure. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p89#2/r9]: Rāzī treats the earth and sky as cosmic evidence that natural bodies themselves depend on a maker; changes such as thunder, lightning, winds, clouds, and seasons are signs of the horizons."}, {"id": "2

{"id": "2:31/q13", "question": "What did God display to the angels?", "turns_on": "Whether the object was the named beings or the names themselves, and how the pronoun and demonstrative bear on it.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q13/p1", "position": "God displayed the named beings, their forms or images.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Akhfash and many exegetes read the masculine pronoun and 'these' as pointing to beings. {"id": "2:31/q14", "question": "How were the displayed beings shown?", "turns_on": "Materially created beings, representative kinds, small particles, mental forms, or unseen realities.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q14/p1", "position": "God represented their images or forms in the angels' minds.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Ṭabrisī allow mental impression before creation; al-Ālūsī allows intellectual forms or an imaginal realm in which abstract meanings take shape."}, {"id": "2:31/q14/p2", "position": "God created the beings and showed their actual forms, possibly one exemplar of each kind.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Ṭabrisī describe visible entities; an exemplar leaves angels less excuse than a description. {"id": "2:31/q15", "question": "Why is the pronoun in ‘displayed them’ masculine plural?", "turns_on": "It may denote rational referents alone, or a mixed group whose rational members govern agreement; other explanations personify or equate names and bearers.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q15/p1", "position": "A group including rational and nonrational beings takes masculine agreement by predominance or honor.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī cites 24:45; al-Zajjāj, al-Jishumī, al-Baghawī, al-Rāzī and later grammarians make mixed-group agreement decisive, so the pronoun need not restrict the scope."}, {"id": "2:31/q15/p2", "position": "It refers to rational beings, especially descendants and angels.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says this is prevailing Arabic usage and therefore favors their names; Elmalılı likewise favors descendants. Others note 24:45 as an exception."}, {"id": "2:31/q15/p3", "position": "The pronoun refers to the names through their bearers or because names and referents are treated as one.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī and al-Ālūsī report metonymy or identity; al-Jishumī and al-Ālūsī reject literal display of abstractions."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q16", "question": "What pronoun readings are reported for ‘displayed them’?", "turns_on": "Masculine plural of the received text versus feminine plural and singular variants.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q16/p1", "position": "Ibn Masʿūd or ʿAbd Allāh reads feminine plural ʿaraḍahunna.", "reasons": "This can point to names or named entities as a nonrational plural; sources differ in their explanation."}, {"id": "2:31/q16/p2", "position": "Ubayy reads feminine singular ʿaraḍahā.", "reasons": "The pronoun can refer to names, named entities, or, in one Ibn Kathīr explanation, heavens."}, {"id": "2:31/q16/p3", "position": "The received reading is masculine plural ʿaraḍahum.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ takes embodied persons as natural; al-Ṭabarī and other exegetes allow mixed kinds by masculine predominance."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q17", "question": "Which angels were shown the beings?", "turns_on": "All angels or the group associated with Iblis.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q17/p1", "position": "The addressed angels were those with Iblis, including his troops in the war against jinn.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās reports this restriction; al-Rāzī's narration connects their prior question to anger and later repentance."}, {"id": "2:31/q17/p2", "position": "The whole company of angels was addressed.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān records this as a possible scope of the definite plural."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q18", "question": "What does ‘inform Me’ mean here?", "turns_on": "Simple informing versus a weighty report that produces knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q18/p1", "position": "It means tell or inform Me of the names.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī cites al-Nābigha's use of anبأ for informing; Ibn ʿAbbās gives the direct gloss. Al-Māwardī relates nabāʾ to report and prophetic title; the verb can take two objects or three through aʿlama."}, {"id": "2:31/q18/p2", "position": "It asks for an important report that conveys knowledge rather than mere utterance.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says some limit nabaʾ to consequential news; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it significant eagerly sought information, and al-Ālūsī says this suits the names' elevated rank."}, {"id": "2:31/q18/p3", "position": "Adam informs the angels but does not teach them his comprehensive knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥaralī says Adam possessed what the angels could receive only as information and lacked capacity to master; Elmalılı distinguishes direct grasp of reality from mediated verbal signs."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q19", "question": "How is ‘inform Me’ read or pronounced?", "turns_on": "Whether the hamza is maintained, softened or elided.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q19/p1", "position": "Al-Aʿmash and another transmitted form elide the hamza: anbūnī.", "reasons": "Qirāʾāt Er explains a dialectal or phonological omission without a change in meaning."}, {"id": "2:31/q19/p2", "position": "The hamza is pronounced in anbiʾūnī, from anبأ yunbiʾu.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās calls it hamzat qaṭʿ and allows softening or replacement."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q20", "question": "What does ‘these’ point to, and how is it parsed?", "turns_on": "Present referents versus names representing absent referents.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q20/p1", "position": "It points to named beings made present in the display.", "reasons": "Al-Mujāhid says these are the taught things; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān argue demonstratives normally point to visible present entities. {"id": "2:31/q23", "question": "Why did God ask angels to give the names?", "turns_on": "Exposing ignorance, displaying Adam's merit, demonstrating fitness for rule, or an impossible command.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q23/p1", "position": "The challenge exposes the angels' ignorance of what is before them and of the unseen future.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash says no prior claim is needed; al-Wāḥidī compares 2:23. {"id": "2:31/q24", "question": "What is the syntax of ‘if you are truthful’?", "turns_on": "Whether the preceding imperative itself is the apodosis or only indicates an omitted one.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q24/p1", "position": "The apodosis is omitted and understood as 'then inform Me.'", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās and Ibn ʿAṭiyya attribute this to al-Mubarrad, but Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn correct the attribution to Sībawayh and most Basrans; al-Samīn says a genuine preceding apodosis would need fāʾ."}, {"id": "2:31/q24/p2", "position": "The preceding imperative is the conditional's answer.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās and Ibn ʿAṭiyya attribute it to Sībawayh; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn assign it instead to the Kufans, Abū Zayd and al-Mubarrad. {"id": "2:31/q25", "question": "Does ‘if’ here mean a condition or ‘when’?", "turns_on": "A temporal paraphrase is reported but rejected by several grammarians.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q25/p1", "position": "It is a genuine condition.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās, al-Ṭabarī, Abū ʿUbayd, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī reject substitution with idh or idhā; they say it removes the clause's conditional force."}, {"id": "2:31/q25/p2", "position": "It means 'when you were' rather than setting a condition.", "reasons": "Reported from some exegetes, but the named grammarians reject it."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q26", "question": "What claim is ‘if you are truthful’ testing?", "turns_on": "Sources connect it to several distinct prior or implied angelic claims, or simply to accuracy in naming.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q26/p1", "position": "Their assumption that God would create none more knowledgeable, honored or excellent than themselves.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda's accounts say they privately boasted of prior worship and precedence; Adam's lesson and their admission correct the assumption."}, {"id": "2:31/q26/p2", "position": "Their forecast that the earthly successor would corrupt and shed blood.", "reasons": "Reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd and Companions connect it to 2:30; inability to know visible names exposes uncertainty about future unseen conduct."}, {"id": "2:31/q26/p3", "position": "Their implicit claim that they deserved vicegerency because of purity, worship or sinlessness.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī mentions their own glorification against another creature's disobedience; al-Bayḍāwī and Asad take purity as the implied claim, and Elmalılı makes governance the test."}, {"id": "2:31/q26/p4", "position": "Their ability to give a correct answer about the names, without a specific earlier boast.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash calls it exposure of ignorance; al-Naqqāsh says the accuracy condition excludes speculative ijtihād, comparing the mistaken guess in 2:259. Abū Ḥayyān says truthful means correct rather than merely non-lying."}, {"id": "2:31/q26/p5", "position": "Their implied judgment that appointing Adam was unfitting for God's wisdom.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī allows truthfulness of an implication in a question; Ibn ʿĀshūr considers whether the angels' words were an objection or a submissive request for explanation."}]}
{"id": "2:31/q27", "question": "What does Adam's lesson show about knowledge and its possessors?", "turns_on": "How the lesson establishes Adam's rank and the value of knowledge relative to worship, authority, and mere labels.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q27/p1", "position": "Divinely taught knowledge gives Adam public honor, priority over angels and fitness for vicegerency.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī contrasts secret teaching with public display; al-Baghawī uses it for prophetic rank over angels. Al-Rāzī argues knowledge, rather than strength or wealth, explains prostration and leadership. Ibn ʿĀshūr connects naming to practical analysis, justice and human governance. Ibn ʿĀshūr links Adam's demonstrated distinction to his fitness as steward and to what the angels did not know."}, {"id": "2:31/q27/p2", "position": "Knowledge is more exalted than uncomprehending worship and demands humility, practice and fear of God.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī contrasts angelic praise with knowing; al-Rāzī adduces 35:28, 39:9, 58:11, 96:1-5, 20:114 and many reports, distinctions among kinds of scholars, and warnings about hoarding, vanity and knowledge without action. Bursevī traces knowledge to love and obedience."}]}

{"id": "2:31/q30", "question": "How does this scene connect to the vicegerency dialogue and surrounding verses?", "turns_on": "Explanations differ about narrative chronology and whether the lesson completes the response of 2:30.", "positions": [{"id": "2:31/q30/p1", "position": "Adam's teaching gives the concrete answer to the angels' concern in 2:30.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān, Ibn Kathīr, al-Ālūsī and others say God moves from general assurance to displayed knowledge.
